baseline_assumptions: Middle-school learner with basic coding; no learner diagnosis observed.
Week 1 is a foundation, not full contest mastery.

goals.description: Reason about shape, axis and array manipulation as a contest foundation.
Use a short function contract, missingness and returned values.
Use the agreed weekly written assessment format.
Relate variance, units and standard deviation to later feature scaling.

comparisons.assessment_method: Review of assigned task text, not observed student work.
comparisons.answer_conditions: Student is asked to hide completed examples and record help; teacher answers are separate but in the same repository.
comparisons.allowed_support: The task asks learners to record assistance; actual assistance and results are unobserved.
comparisons.competency: Distinguish axis exchange from a reshape with the same resulting shape.
comparisons.difference: The original lacked a same-shape operation choice; the candidate asks students to predict two results, identify differing positions and justify which operation swaps axes.
comparisons.rationale: A reviewer found this scoped teaching design present; no student performance or contest equivalence is claimed.

theory.claim: Shape alone does not fix how input positions map to output positions.

problem_refs.locator: Multiple-choice question 24 on feature engineering; high-school example, not a direct week-1 question

comparisons.difference: The candidate adds a worked cm-to-mm comparison, a standard-deviation bridge and changed-condition questions; this is an introductory bridge to later preprocessing rather than mastery of feature engineering.
comparisons.rationale: Independent calculation confirms the scoped explanation and tasks; their learning effect is unobserved.

theory.claim: Shifting all values leaves population variance unchanged; multiplication by 2 multiplies variance by 4; standard deviation has the original unit.
